Analytical methods Prior to quantification of PFAS concentration in samples, samples were purified using solid phase extraction (SPE) to remove high con - centration of inorganic salt. The Water Oasis Wax weak-ion-exchange SPE cartridges (3 mL, 60 mg sorbent) were first conditioned by running 5 mL of a 0.1 % (0.028 M) NH 4 OH in MeOH through them. Next, 5 mL of MeOH was used to rinse the cartridges, followed by 5 mL of Milli-Q water. Once the conditioning step was completed, 10 mL of samples were shaken vigorously and then loaded onto the cartridges. A flowrate of 2 drops per second was used for the loading process. The cartridges were then washed with 10 mL of a 25 mM sodium acetate solution. Finally, the cartridges were eluted with 5 mL of MeOH and 5 mL of 0.1 % (0.028 M) NH 4 OH in MeOH solution, respectively. To determine the extent of degradation, the samples were analyzed using an Agilent 1200 series ultra-high performance liquid chromatography/ mass spectrometry (uHPLC/MS) instrument. The details of PFAS detection method are provided in Text S.2.

text: Conclusion An eﬃcient and convenient SPME method was developed for PFAS in aqueous matrices and applied to river, lake, tap and bottled water samples. HLB-WAX/PAN SPME extraction phase was highly selective for PFAS and thus has greater potential for use in fur- ther studies of more complex samples in light of its biocompati- bility. The EPA health advisory level for PFOA and PFOS is 70 ng L − 1 while GenX and PFBS are currently still being evaluated by EPA and other environmental agencies. This developed proto- col achieved LOQs of 1 –2 . 5 ng L − 1 for the model analytes with a sample volume of only 1.5 mL, demonstrating the eﬃcacy of pre-concentration offered by SPME for PFAS. Furthermore, the pre-concentration effects augmented method sensitivity far greater than dilute-and-shoot methods, which is widely employed by reg- ulatory agencies for PFAS analysis. No substantial matrix effects from water samples were observed for PFBS and GenX. Through the use of the developed protocol, a highly sensitive quantita- tive analysis can be performed for PFAS of varying physicochem- ical properties, achieving LOQs below current EPA drinking water health advisories. doc_id: 2025 - Capodaglio - Prospects of Novel Technologies for PFAS Destruction in Water and Wastewater.pdf
text: AORP methods (photocatalysis, EAOP , NTP , E- beam), pyrolysis, and SCWO have been proposed to achieve the final destruction of PFAS compounds. Ongoing research aims at reducing the cost of these technologies and improving their destruction efficiency; commercial PFAS destruction methods have been introduced recently, but their full-scale application is still unreported in the scientific literature. Concerns about the potential for some PFASs and precursors to break through current treatment methods, the partial degradation of targeted compounds to non-targeted ones, and potentially dangerous by-products have not been dismissed yet, due to the non- detectability of a large number of PFAS molecules beyond those targeted by regulations. Incomplete and uncertain degradation pathways following destructive treatment also raise issues about overall risk reduction. A major challenge for the assessment of an effective reduction in PFAS contamination is related to the standardization of their quantification methodologies and to the development of analytical advancements to allow for the identification of PFAS congeners following specific treatments and fine-tune both removal and destructive remediation technologies. Generally speaking, the most effective technologies for breaking down PFASs are those that can rapidly deliver high energy into a contaminated solution, in order to overcome the high C-F bond strength and avoid by-product accumulation during the destruction process.

The review focuses on adsorption-based removal technologies, in-depth evaluating mechanisms of PFAS interactions with adsorbents such as activated carbon, biochar, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and ion-exchange resins. A comparative analysis of these materials considers their removal efficiencies, operational constraints and energy demands. Furthermore, the review also identifies challenges and knowledge gaps, including the need for improved mechanistic understanding, standardised testing and long-term performance data. Looking ahead, the article discusses future directions for PFAS remediation, including the development of advanced hybrid adsorbents, the integration of machine learning for material design and the alignment of scientific innovation with policy. The review concludes with recommendations for harmonised regulations and interdisciplinary collaboration to support sustainable and effective PFAS mitigation efforts. text: PFAS are used in laboratory research to produce artificially contaminated feed water for convenience of measurement. The most commonly used for PFAS are adsorption (including ion exchange), membrane filtration, and degra- dation (Table 1). Adsorption is the simplest of these methods and relatively inexpensive (Lei et al. 2023). However, the cost and treatment time for adsorption increases if a strict removal rate needs to be achieved. Membrane treatment ensures a good removal rate for the permeate (T. Lee et al. 2022) but the energy needed to generate filtration pressure makes membrane treatment more expensive than adsorp- tion. Both adsorption and filtration concentrate, but do not destroy, PFAS. Degradation could be used to destroy PFAS, but high energy is needed to rupture PFAS molecules. Therefore, degradation is also expensive. Filtration treatment costs could be reduced by developing a membrane with a high permeable flux that maintains the PFAS blocking rate. Many general reviews have recently been published on PFAS treatment. Most existing reviews (Saawarn et al. 2022; Wanninayake 2021; Yadav et al. 2022) summarize different PFAS treatment methods, among which only a few studies on membrane-based methods are included. Activated carbon becomes costly due to frequent regeneration needs- especially at high PFAS loads-and competes with co- contaminants, while membrane systems concentrate PFAS into waste brines requiring further treatment. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) such as electrochemical oxidation, ozonation, UV-based systems, and supercritical water oxidation aim to degrade PFAS rather than separate them 15,16. Regeneration of spent adsorbent after PFAS adsorption Managing spent adsorbents presents environmental and economic challenges, primarily due to the risk of rein- troducing PFAS into the environment during disposal or regeneration. Advanced regeneration techniques, such as microwave, chemical, thermal, and hydrothermal treatments, have shown promising potential, achieving up to w99 % regeneration efﬁciency for PFAS-laden carbon-based composites [ 50]. Chemical regeneration is particularly effective for multicomponent regenerates and has demonstrated durability over ﬁve consecutive adsorptionedesorption cycles. However, combining chemical regeneration with advanced degradation sys- tems, while effective, often reduces PFAS adsorption capacity by 5 e10 % due to irreversible adsorption and pore blocking. Thermal regeneration, performed at high temperatures (/C21700e800 /C14C), has proven effective but is unsuitable for certain adsorbents, such as ion- exchange resins, due to structural degradation under extreme conditions. These limitations highlight the need for innovative, cost-effective regeneration strate- gies tailored to the speciﬁc properties of adsorbents and the type of PFAS contamination being addressed. text: Among a number of remediation technologies, adsorption has been demonstrated to be a manageable and cost-effective method for the removal of PFASs in aqueous media. text: In this study, we demonstrate a simple way to activate and reactivate biochar to effectively remove PFAS from water. The approach utilizes air as the activating gas at moderate temperature (400 °C) in a muffle furnace. We have shown previously that post-pyrolysis hot air oxidation improves sorption affinity and capacity for (heterocyclic) aromatic compounds. 55,56 In this research communication, we report that this treatment boosts the affinity of softwood-derived biochar for certain PFAS by up to 3 orders of magnitude compared with the original biochar. Furthermore, we show that the biochar can be reactivated by brief thermal treatment in air at 500 °C, which removes the sorbed PFAS and renders the biochar even more strongly sorptive in a second use. ■ MATERIALS AND METHODS We prepared biochars by a reported method 61 in which softwood (SW; mixed species) or hardwood (M; maple) shavings were pyrolyzed at a final heat treatment temperature (HTT) of 300, 400, or 600 °C for 2 h with N 2 flow. We then thermally oxidized a portion of the thus-prepared biochars at 400 °C for 30 min in air headspace (“post-pyrolysis air oxidation,” PPAO). 62−64 Biochars are labeled MXXX or SWXXX or MXXX-PPAO or SWXXX-PPAO, where XXX is the HTT.

text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. The removal of PFAS by GAC can be explained by several mecha - nisms, including hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic attraction, and PFAS aggregation ( Du et al., 2014 ). PFAS compounds vary significantly in hydrophobicity: carbon chain length is proportional to hydropho - bicity, and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) demonstrate increased hydrophobicity as compared to perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) with the same perfluorinated carbon chain length ( Park et al., 2020 ). As such, GAC treatment has been found to be more effective for removing longer-chain PFAS than shorter-chain ones, and more effective for removing PFSA than PFCA ( McCleaf et al., 2017; Westreich et al., 2018 ). Traditional full-scale GAC treatment facility design is typically based on empty bed contact time (EBCT) and media service-life, often described by the number of bed volumes (BVs) the system can treat until solute breakthrough ( Crittenden et al., 1987 ). Contact time is considered an important design parameter for sorption because it is crucial that the contact time is long enough to fully sorb the target contaminants ( Murray et al., 2021 , Pannu et al., 2024 ). Failure to optimize contact time can result in either inefficient removal of target contaminants or unnecessary cost of oper - ation. Therefore, selection of the appropriate contact time is essential for testing and scale-up of novel sorbents ( Murphy et al., 2023 ). The rec - ommended full-scale contact time for removing PFAS by conventional adsorbents is well studied, with a recommended contact time of 2 – 5 min for IX resins and 10 – 30 min for GAC ( Pannu et al., 2024 ). However, the optimal contact time is unknown for novel adsorbents. Therefore, this study focuses on understanding how contact time impacts breakthrough of contaminant mixtures in packed beds of StyDex in wastewater, and the implications for scaling-up to pilot and full-scale operations. Supercritical water has a relatively high density compared to water vapor at ambient conditions (approximately one- third of the den - sity of liquid water at atmospheric conditions). In this study, the C/H/O/ F ReaxFF force field developed is used to simulate the reaction behavior of PFNA under pyrolysis and SCWO conditions. Two classes of PFAS, perfluoroalkyl car - boxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), are commonly found in legacy stockpiles, in - dustrial waste streams, and as environmental pollutants. Continuous flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) reactors have been shown to destroy several PFAS and aqueous film-forming foams. However, a direct com - parison of the SCWO efficacy for PFSAs and PFCAs has not been reported. We show the effectiveness of continuous flow SCWO treatment for a matrix of model PFCAs and PFSAs as a function of operating temperature. PFSAs appear to be significantly more recalcitrant than PFCAs in the SCWO environment. The SCWO treatment results in a destruction and removal efficiency of 99.999% at a T > 610 ◦ C and at a residence time of ~30 s. Introduction Water above 374°C and 22.1 MPa becomes supercritical, a special phase of water with both liquid-like and gas-like properties. Above the critical point of water, most organic compounds are soluble, oxygen is fully miscible, and salts are insoluble ( Hodes et al. 2004 ; V oisin et al. 2017). In the presence of an oxidizing agent, such as oxygen, supercritical water ’s unique properties accelerate the oxidation of a broad range of organic pollutants. Since the 1980s, supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) has been used successfully to treat a variety of hazardous wastes, such as chemical warfare agents and halogenated compounds ( Abeln et al. 2001 ; Cohen et al. 1998 ; Kim et al. 2010 ). Technical challenges have limited implementation of SCWO at scale, including the buildup of corro- sive species during the oxidation reaction and salts’ precipitation on the reactor body, leading to high maintenance and operation costs (Marrone 2013; Mitton et al. 2001 ). This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. In contrast, destructive technologies can convert primary pollutants into more hazardous secondary Environments 2025, 12, 330 4 of 34 byproducts, creating additional challenges. Second, adsorption is simple in both the syn- thesis of adsorbents and their use. This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. In contrast, destructive technologies can convert primary pollutants into more hazardous secondary Environments 2025, 12, 330 4 of 34 byproducts, creating additional challenges. These results highlight a bene ﬁcial in ﬂuence on adsorption ki- netics on PFAS adsorption, where with higher EBCT the water spends more time in contact with GAC particles and thus PFASs and other substances have more time to diffuse into pores and adsorb onto sorption sites. This might further relate to diffusion limitations “older” GAC ﬁlters experience, due to the total organic matter loading. Contact time and adsorption kinetics Adsorption kinetics influence the practicality of PFAS removal, especially in flow-through systems. Traditional adsorbents such as PAC often require extended contact times (up to several hours) to reach equilibrium (Son and An 2022). By contrast, nano-engineered adsorbents and hybrid materials, due to their high surface-to-volume ratios and reactive interfaces, tend to exhibit rapid uptake, often reaching equilibrium within min - utes (Birch et al. 2022). Rapid adsorption kinetics are essential for developing efficient point-of-use treatment technologies and scaling up continuous treatment systems. NOM may introduce steric hindrance, reduce porosity through fouling or shift surface charges, thereby diminishing PFAS removal efficiency (Qi et al. 2022). Strategies such as pre-filtration, adsorbent surface modification or the development of anti-fouling materials can help mitigate these effects and improve per - formance in natural water matrices. text: This study investigated the sorption of per- and polyfluorinated-alkyl substances (PFAS) onto granular activated carbon (GAC). The study was performed at environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations and a realistic water-to-GAC ratio, providing a realism often overlooked in existing studies. Three different forms of GAC were evaluated, differing in micropore and mesopore structures. Tap water spiked with 5 ng/L of each of 31 PFAS was used in the sorption experiments, i.e. perfluorocarboxylic acids (C 4 – C 12 ), perfluorosulfonic acids (PFSA, C 5 – C 10 ) including linear and branched isomers, and three groups of PFAS precursors (per-/polyfluoroalkyl ether acids, sulfonamides, and sulfonamide acetic acids). The three studied GAC did not exhibit distinct differences in PFAS sorption. The removal of PFAS was below 50 % for most studied PFAS, except for the short-chain PFAS precursors. Sorption was affected by both the carbon chain length and functional groups for PFAS, while this was not observed for PFAS precursors. The presence of ether linkages and sulfonamide groups notably enhanced sorption. Linear and branched PFSA demonstrated similar sorption behavior, whereas branched isomers of the sulfonamide acetic acid precursors exhibited significantly higher sorp - tion. This indicates that sorption was determined by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions.

text: Findings from this study examined for the ﬁrst time the adsorption of 75 PFASs from an AFFF mixture to 14 adsorbents (13 resins and GAC) at environmentally relevant concentrations. Results from this work show that AERs with polystyrene backbones are more selective toward PFASs compared to GAC, especially for the short-chain PFAAs (e.g., PFBA). Furthermore, by comparing the selectivity coe ﬃ cients of each PFAS −AER combination, the physical characteristics of AERs (i.e., polymer matrix, functional group, and morphology) were found to strongly inﬂuence their a ﬃ nity and capacity toward the 75 PFASs. For example, while macroporous AERs were found to exhibit a much higher maximum PFOS capacity compared to gel-type AERs, AERs that contain more hydrophobic polymer matrices (e.g., polystyrene) and functional groups (e.g., quaternary ammonium with long alkyl branches) tend to display stronger selectivity toward PFASs compared to other AERs that lack these properties. These ﬁndings con ﬁrm that rather than electrostatic interactions alone driving the adsorption process, nonelectrostatic interactions (e.g., hydrophobic interaction) played an important role in controlling the extent to which individual PFASs adsorb to di ﬀerent resins. Such ﬁndings are valuable assets for developing more e ﬀective AERs to treat the wide range of PFASs detected in the environment.

In all methods, the cleanup of extract to eliminate interfering organic and inorganic compounds prior to LC-MS/MS analysis is critical to obtaining acceptable chromatogram quality and recoveries of PFAS from these complex matrices. While a variety of adsorbents have been employed in the cleanup step, we argue that a “one-size-fits- all” method may not exist. Specifically, in this study, we observed that none of the existing methods could prevent precipitate formation when methanolic extracts from the five studied biosolids were reconstituted with water. Centrifugation and filtration of the reconstituted extracts to remove precipitates did not sufficiently eliminate interferences to allow PFAS quantification. To overcome this issue, the use of blends of adsorbents (ENVI-Carb, PSA, C18) with different adsorptive properties that could remove a broader range of interfering substances was evaluated. A blend consisting of 1000 mg ENVI-Carb, 500 mg PSA and 500 mg C18 was used to successfully analyze PFAS in the six studied biosolids. While this adsorbent formulation shows considerable promise, the optimum formulation could be sample-specific, given that sludges and biosolids vary widely in characteristics.

text: Electrochemical oxidation is generally employed downstream of concentration technologies such as IXR or foam fractionation rather than being applied directly to PFAS- impacted groundwater. This treatment sequence reflects several key constraints at environmentally relevant concen- trations. First, PFAS levels in groundwater typically span the ng L −1 to μg L −1 range, where mass transfer limitations restrict removal efficiency at the electrode surface. Second, the direct application of electrochemical oxidation to groundwater would require prohibitively large electrode areas and high energy input given the large water volumes involved, whereas treatment of concentrated residual streams enables more efficient operation. Third, because PFAS degradation by electrochemical oxidation follows approximately first-order kinetics, higher influent concentrations (mg L −1 ) are associated with reduced specific energy demand compared to μg L −1 influent levels. Finally, the increased solution conductivity of concentrated waste streams alleviates ionic limitations and enhances the effective active area of the reactor, thereby improving overall treatment performance. text: AORP methods (photocatalysis, EAOP , NTP , E- beam), pyrolysis, and SCWO have been proposed to achieve the final destruction of PFAS compounds. Ongoing research aims at reducing the cost of these technologies and improving their destruction efficiency; commercial PFAS destruction methods have been introduced recently, but their full-scale application is still unreported in the scientific literature. Concerns about the potential for some PFASs and precursors to break through current treatment methods, the partial degradation of targeted compounds to non-targeted ones, and potentially dangerous by-products have not been dismissed yet, due to the non- detectability of a large number of PFAS molecules beyond those targeted by regulations. Incomplete and uncertain degradation pathways following destructive treatment also raise issues about overall risk reduction. A major challenge for the assessment of an effective reduction in PFAS contamination is related to the standardization of their quantification methodologies and to the development of analytical advancements to allow for the identification of PFAS congeners following specific treatments and fine-tune both removal and destructive remediation technologies. Generally speaking, the most effective technologies for breaking down PFASs are those that can rapidly deliver high energy into a contaminated solution, in order to overcome the high C-F bond strength and avoid by-product accumulation during the destruction process.

In contrast, column studies better represent field conditions, supporting continuous pollutant removal, flow dynamics, and regener - ation studies. However, equilibrium in column studies is achieved only after the breakthrough point due to shorter contact times ( Sazali et al., 2020 ). Numerous studies have utilized batch and column experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of various biochars in treating different pol - lutants, providing comprehensive insights into the versatility of biochar in treatment applications. Huang et al. (2022a) reported a maximum sorption density of 2200 mg/kg for Al-modified bamboo biochar in a batch study, where the removal of sulfonamides occurred through electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic effects, and π - π interactions. While in the fixed-column study, the highest removal efficiency was achieved with a 1000 mg dose at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. The break - through model revealed that the adsorption process was primarily controlled by solid surface mass transfer and diffusion mechanisms.

The review focuses on adsorption-based removal technologies, in-depth evaluating mechanisms of PFAS interactions with adsorbents such as activated carbon, biochar, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and ion-exchange resins. text: This study investigated the sorption of per- and polyfluorinated-alkyl substances (PFAS) onto granular activated carbon (GAC). The study was performed at environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations and a realistic water-to-GAC ratio, providing a realism often overlooked in existing studies. Three different forms of GAC were evaluated, differing in micropore and mesopore structures. Tap water spiked with 5 ng/L of each of 31 PFAS was used in the sorption experiments, i.e. perfluorocarboxylic acids (C 4 – C 12 ), perfluorosulfonic acids (PFSA, C 5 – C 10 ) including linear and branched isomers, and three groups of PFAS precursors (per-/polyfluoroalkyl ether acids, sulfonamides, and sulfonamide acetic acids). The three studied GAC did not exhibit distinct differences in PFAS sorption. The removal of PFAS was below 50 % for most studied PFAS, except for the short-chain PFAS precursors. Sorption was affected by both the carbon chain length and functional groups for PFAS, while this was not observed for PFAS precursors. The presence of ether linkages and sulfonamide groups notably enhanced sorption. Linear and branched PFSA demonstrated similar sorption behavior, whereas branched isomers of the sulfonamide acetic acid precursors exhibited significantly higher sorp - tion. This indicates that sorption was determined by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions.

text: PFAS are used in laboratory research to produce artificially contaminated feed water for convenience of measurement. The most commonly used for PFAS are adsorption (including ion exchange), membrane filtration, and degra- dation (Table 1). Adsorption is the simplest of these methods and relatively inexpensive (Lei et al. 2023). However, the cost and treatment time for adsorption increases if a strict removal rate needs to be achieved. Membrane treatment ensures a good removal rate for the permeate (T. Lee et al. 2022) but the energy needed to generate filtration pressure makes membrane treatment more expensive than adsorp- tion. Both adsorption and filtration concentrate, but do not destroy, PFAS. Degradation could be used to destroy PFAS, but high energy is needed to rupture PFAS molecules. Therefore, degradation is also expensive. Filtration treatment costs could be reduced by developing a membrane with a high permeable flux that maintains the PFAS blocking rate. Many general reviews have recently been published on PFAS treatment. Most existing reviews (Saawarn et al. 2022; Wanninayake 2021; Yadav et al. 2022) summarize different PFAS treatment methods, among which only a few studies on membrane-based methods are included. It is possible to remove PFAS from water by either separating these compounds or destruct- ing them partially or completely. Thus, the ability of membrane technologies to remove PFAS in water and wastewater systems is a promising research and application topic [ 10 , 23 ]. Membrane separation processes are widely applied in water/waste - water treatment and industries and it was found to be effective in rejecting short and long chain PFAS with efficiencies exceeding 90 % [ 24 , 25 ]. Generally, in membrane separation systems, feed water con - taining PFAS molecules is rejected by the membrane (semi-permeable selective barrier) while water molecules are passing to the permeation side of the system. The most famous, effective and largely investigated membrane systems for PFAS removal are pressure driven membrane systems, particularly nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) sys - tems. The defined removal mechanism are size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution diffusion for NF and RO, respectively. The effi - ciency of these membranes in rejecting PFASs from aqueous environ - ments were reported to approach 99 % [ 26 , 27 ]. Despite the maturity level of the NF and RO systems and simplicity in application, the major drawback experienced is treatment of rejected streams containing high PFAS concentration which requires further attention by coupling membrane separation with other processes such as adsorption or AOPs.

In these cases, the treatment meth- odology is multistep requiring additional expenditure of energy along with cost associated with complexity. Direct decomposition is desirable in that ideally it does not create an additional waste stream; rather, the compound is disassembled chemically to harm- less by-products. Key questions regarding PFAS treatment include what is the fate of the shorter chains produced, and is the advanced method also appropriate to treat these shorter chains? Such ques- tions have not been settled to date. 8 In this work, plasma treatment is applied to the treatment of PFAS-contaminated ground water. While plasma treatment is often thought of as an advanced oxidation method, it has been shown that oxidation is not effective in decomposing short chain PFAS compounds. 8 This is largely due the relative strength of the C –F bond and the high electronegativity of fluorine. The oxidation potential of fluorine is larger than that of OH, the chief radical in advanced oxidation. Reduction methods, on the other hand, have shown success at defluorinating and ultimately decomposing PFAS compounds. 9 These methods feature solvated electrons —a short lived, highly reactive complex that destabilizes PFAS compounds.

A wide range of technologies has been developed to address PFAS contamination, including adsorption using activated carbon 12,13 and membrane separation 14. While effective at capturing PFAS, these methods are non- destructive and generate secondary waste streams. Activated carbon becomes costly due to frequent regeneration needs- especially at high PFAS loads-and competes with co- contaminants, while membrane systems concentrate PFAS into waste brines requiring further treatment. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) such as electrochemical oxidation, ozonation, UV-based systems, and supercritical water oxidation aim to degrade PFAS rather than separate them 15,16. The recalcitrant behavior of PFAS to most traditional water treatment processes calls for development of novel or modified treatment approaches for effective PFAS elimination. Currently, high- pressure membrane systems, including nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) are among the most promising and readily applied technologies for PFAS removal. In this review, we summarized peer-reviewed scientific articles on the development and use of 20 different types of commercial and 6 synthesized/modified NF and RO membranes in terms of PFAS removal efficacy. Synthesizing of existing knowledge shows that under environmentally relevant pH and concentration, NF and RO can effectively remove PFAS from water. The impact of PFAS molecular weight (MW) and functionality, membrane characteristics, feed water constitution, natural organic matters and operational conditions were systematically reviewed and evaluated. Moving forward, we recommend additional research dedicated to understanding the behaviors of PFAS alternatives and other over - looked compounds (e.g., PFAS with chain length C 2 and C3) during NF and RO processes. Further, it is critical to develop or optimize existing membrane products with strong selectivity for specific PFAS species, while being resistant to fouling. Overall, this review is expected to assist researchers and water quality managers investi - gating membrane processes for PFAS removal. 1. Introduction 1.1. Background

Regeneration of spent adsorbent after PFAS adsorption Managing spent adsorbents presents environmental and economic challenges, primarily due to the risk of rein- troducing PFAS into the environment during disposal or regeneration. Advanced regeneration techniques, such as microwave, chemical, thermal, and hydrothermal treatments, have shown promising potential, achieving up to w99 % regeneration efﬁciency for PFAS-laden carbon-based composites [ 50]. Chemical regeneration is particularly effective for multicomponent regenerates and has demonstrated durability over ﬁve consecutive adsorptionedesorption cycles. However, combining chemical regeneration with advanced degradation sys- tems, while effective, often reduces PFAS adsorption capacity by 5 e10 % due to irreversible adsorption and pore blocking. Thermal regeneration, performed at high temperatures (/C21700e800 /C14C), has proven effective but is unsuitable for certain adsorbents, such as ion- exchange resins, due to structural degradation under extreme conditions. These limitations highlight the need for innovative, cost-effective regeneration strate- gies tailored to the speciﬁc properties of adsorbents and the type of PFAS contamination being addressed. text: Among a number of remediation technologies, adsorption has been demonstrated to be a manageable and cost-effective method for the removal of PFASs in aqueous media. Batch sorption tests (24 h) were carried out to evaluate the removal efficiency of each PFAS substance in relation to the two biochars. text: In this study, we demonstrate a simple way to activate and reactivate biochar to effectively remove PFAS from water. The approach utilizes air as the activating gas at moderate temperature (400 °C) in a muffle furnace. We have shown previously that post-pyrolysis hot air oxidation improves sorption affinity and capacity for (heterocyclic) aromatic compounds. 55,56 In this research communication, we report that this treatment boosts the affinity of softwood-derived biochar for certain PFAS by up to 3 orders of magnitude compared with the original biochar. Furthermore, we show that the biochar can be reactivated by brief thermal treatment in air at 500 °C, which removes the sorbed PFAS and renders the biochar even more strongly sorptive in a second use. ■ MATERIALS AND METHODS We prepared biochars by a reported method 61 in which softwood (SW; mixed species) or hardwood (M; maple) shavings were pyrolyzed at a final heat treatment temperature (HTT) of 300, 400, or 600 °C for 2 h with N 2 flow. We then thermally oxidized a portion of the thus-prepared biochars at 400 °C for 30 min in air headspace (“post-pyrolysis air oxidation,” PPAO). 62−64 Biochars are labeled MXXX or SWXXX or MXXX-PPAO or SWXXX-PPAO, where XXX is the HTT.

text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. Supercritical Water Oxidation SCWO leverages the supercritical phase of water that is achieved by increasing the temperature and pressure of a water- based liquid to a minimum of 374 °C and 218 atm, respectively, as demonstrated in Figure  2. Supercritical water has a relatively high density compared to water vapor at ambient conditions (approximately one- third of the den - sity of liquid water at atmospheric conditions). In this phase, oxygen is fully soluble, resulting in rapid and complete oxi- dation of organics and transforming the feedstock into car - bon dioxide (CO2), water, and inorganic salts, as shown in Figure  3. When SCWO is applied to PFAS, organic fluorine is mineralized to inorganic fluoride. A major advantage of SCWO over other PFAS destruction technologies is its abil- ity to destroy lower molecular weight, shorter chain PFAS compounds (6 carbon chain structures, or C6, and below) in addition to higher molecular weight, legacy PFAS com - pounds (8 carbon chain structures, or C8, and above). text: Supercritical water ReaxFF Molecular dynamics simulations ABSTRACT Perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), often referred to as one of the "forever chemicals", is found globally, and su - percritical water oxidation (SCWO) presents a promising method for their degradation. In this study, the C/H/O/ F ReaxFF force field developed is used to simulate the reaction behavior of PFNA under pyrolysis and SCWO conditions. The initial decomposition pathway, main intermediates, and product formation mechanisms were elucidated. During pyrolysis, PFNA rapidly decomposed to form intermediates such as CHO 2 and COF, which subsequently formed CO and CO 2 via free radical reactions. The maximum conversion rates for CO and CO 2 reached 18.7%. In SCWO conditions, the combination of high temperature, high pressure, and an oxygen environment significantly accelerated the breakage of fluorine-carbon bonds and the mineralization of carbon components. CHO 2 and COF intermediates were further oxidized by free radicals such as OH and CF 2 . In SCW conditions, the conversion of PFNA reached 23.78%, exceeding the pyrolysis conversion rate by 5.08%. Two classes of PFAS, perfluoroalkyl car - boxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), are commonly found in legacy stockpiles, in - dustrial waste streams, and as environmental pollutants. Continuous flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) reactors have been shown to destroy several PFAS and aqueous film-forming foams. However, a direct com - parison of the SCWO efficacy for PFSAs and PFCAs has not been reported. We show the effectiveness of continuous flow SCWO treatment for a matrix of model PFCAs and PFSAs as a function of operating temperature. PFSAs appear to be significantly more recalcitrant than PFCAs in the SCWO environment. The SCWO treatment results in a destruction and removal efficiency of 99.999% at a T > 610 ◦ C and at a residence time of ~30 s. Fluoride recovery lags destruction PFAS at 510 ◦ C and reaches > 100% above 610 ◦ C, confirming the formation of liquid and gaseous phase intermediate product during lower temperature oxidation. Introduction Water above 374°C and 22.1 MPa becomes supercritical, a special phase of water with both liquid-like and gas-like properties. Above the critical point of water, most organic compounds are soluble, oxygen is fully miscible, and salts are insoluble ( Hodes et al. 2004 ; V oisin et al. 2017). In the presence of an oxidizing agent, such as oxygen, supercritical water ’s unique properties accelerate the oxidation of a broad range of organic pollutants. Since the 1980s, supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) has been used successfully to treat a variety of hazardous wastes, such as chemical warfare agents and halogenated compounds ( Abeln et al. 2001 ; Cohen et al. 1998 ; Kim et al. 2010 ). Technical challenges have limited implementation of SCWO at scale, including the buildup of corro- sive species during the oxidation reaction and salts’ precipitation on the reactor body, leading to high maintenance and operation costs (Marrone 2013; Mitton et al. 2001 ). Higher temperatures are needed to achieve higher destruction efficiencies, which translates to longer heat-up times, and increased energy inputs. From a thermodynamic standpoint, the energetic requirements for SCWO are comparable to incineration of wet wastes. Under atmospheric conditions ~2600 kJ/kg of energy input is required to heat and evap - orate water from 20 ◦ C to 100 ◦ C, while heating and pressurizing water from 20 ◦ C to the supercritical phase at 25 MPa and 500 ◦ C requires ~3060 kJ/kg ( Lemmon et al., 2018 ). Under oxidizing conditions, both SCWO and incineration valorize the energetic content of the feedstock to reduce overall energy demand. SCWO does not produce particulate matter (PM), NO x or SO 2 as reaction products due to the lower operating temperatures, which eliminates the emission treatment requirements on industrial incinerators. In light of these findings, continuous SCWO processing seems more promising than batch SCWO processing as an end-of-life disposal process for PFAS-rich wastes. Continuous SCWO processing requires the PFAS to be contained in a liquid matrix with low salt content to avoid issues with scaling and corrosion.

Many regeneration processes, particularly solvent-based and certain chemical approaches, can achieve initial desorption efficiencies above 90%, but still leave 20–40% of the original PFAS load in the adsorbent, particularly for long-chain PFASs [25,83,104,156,182]. This residual loading can cause pre- mature breakthrough in service, risking exceedances of the PFAS limits unless regeneration cycles are more effective or more frequent. Thermal destruction, while capable of >95% Water 2025, 17, 2813 18 of 28 PFAS mineralisation under controlled laboratory conditions, raises concerns regarding the scalability and completeness of destruction under real-world conditions, particularly with respect to HF and other fluorinated by-products that require advanced flue gas cleaning to meet POPs Regulation requirements [23,52,78,133,134]. EU environmental policy implicitly demands that PFAS releases are prevented not only during water treatment but also during all handling, regeneration, and end-of-life management steps. Supercritical water treatment Above its critical point (T c = 374 ◦ C, P c = 22.1 MPa), water becomes a non-polar solvent, which can efficiently dissolve organic substances and gases [36] . The ion product constant of supercritical water (SCW) is over five orders of magnitude lower than that of water at ambient conditions, facilitating free radical reaction pathways [37] which have been utilized in gasification [38 – 40] , partial oxidation [41] , and SCWO [42 – 44] processes. SCWO process benefits from the high free radical environment to convert organic compounds via oxidative reaction mechanisms into CO 2 and H 2 O, with the hydroxyl radical (OH*) being the primary oxidizing species [45 – 49] . Heteroatoms are converted to corresponding inorganic acids or salts, such as HCl, HF, sulfates, phosphates, etc. High-density homogeneous SCWO environment facilitates fast and more complete oxidative reactions. Water as the reaction medium allows for simulta - neous oxidation and hydrolysis mechanisms [50] , enabling the more complete destruction of some recalcitrant wastes.

This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. In contrast, destructive technologies can convert primary pollutants into more hazardous secondary Environments 2025, 12, 330 4 of 34 byproducts, creating additional challenges. Second, adsorption is simple in both the syn- thesis of adsorbents and their use. text: adsorption The adsorption behaviour of PFASs is primarily dictated by their molecular structure, including chain length, functional head groups (e.g. carboxylate or sulfonate) and amphiphilic nature (Bezerra de Souza et al. 2025). Long-chain PFASs, such as PFOA and PFOS, tend to exhibit stronger adsorption affinities than their short-chain counterparts due to their increased hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals forces (Leung et al. 2023). Their amphiphilic structure (com - prising a hydrophobic perfluoroalkyl tail and a polar func - tional head) enables interaction with both non-polar and charged surfaces depending on environmental pH and ionic strength (Leung et al. 2023). Additionally, the resistance of PFASs to degradation and their unique surface activity influ - ence their interaction with various adsorbent materials. Factors such as the surface charge, porosity and functiona - lisation of the adsorbent surface play a critical role in deter - mining the overall removal efficiency (Mane et al. 2024). This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. The central conclusion of this work is that mass balance must anchor all PFAS strategies. Concentration‐based assessments are insufficient because they obscure internal cycling, precursor transformation, and enrichment processes that influence PFAS distribution. Mass balance identifies leverage points, clarifies where interventions will have meaningful impact, and avoids investment in technologies that treat only a small fraction of the total PFAS mass. Without this perspective, PFAS decisions risk being reactive, incomplete, or misaligned with the flows that drive environmental outcomes. This paper also emphasizes that PFAS management cannot rely on end‐of‐pipe controls alone. The removal of PFAS by GAC can be explained by several mecha - nisms, including hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic attraction, and PFAS aggregation ( Du et al., 2014 ). PFAS compounds vary significantly in hydrophobicity: carbon chain length is proportional to hydropho - bicity, and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) demonstrate increased hydrophobicity as compared to perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) with the same perfluorinated carbon chain length ( Park et al., 2020 ). As such, GAC treatment has been found to be more effective for removing longer-chain PFAS than shorter-chain ones, and more effective for removing PFSA than PFCA ( McCleaf et al., 2017; Westreich et al., 2018 ). Traditional full-scale GAC treatment facility design is typically based on empty bed contact time (EBCT) and media service-life, often described by the number of bed volumes (BVs) the system can treat until solute breakthrough ( Crittenden et al., 1987 ). Rapid small-scale column tests (RSSCTs) were conducted according to the proportional diffusivity (PD) design to assess their suitability to predict full- or pilot-scale GAC performance. PFAA removal from groundwater (GW) and coagulated surface water (SW) was studied with two sub-bituminous coal-based GACs. In batch tests conducted with pulverized GAC, the GACs performed similarly in GW, but the GAC with the larger mesopore volume was more effective for PFAA removal from SW. In column tests, carbon use rates decreased with increasing PFAA chain length and were lower for GW (total organic carbon [TOC] = 0.7 mg/L) than for SW (TOC = 2.0–2.7 mg/L). The volume of SW that could be treated to 10% or 50% PFAA breakthrough was about 50 –60% of the volume of GW that could be treated when comparing pilot-scale data for SW with full-scale data for GW. Consistent differences in PFAA adsorption capacity were not observed for empty bed contact times of 13 and 26 min in full-scale adsorbers treating GW. The PD-RSSCT simulating PFAA removal from GW consistently overpredicted full-scale adsorption capacity, on average by ~70%.

These results highlight a bene ﬁcial in ﬂuence on adsorption ki- netics on PFAS adsorption, where with higher EBCT the water spends more time in contact with GAC particles and thus PFASs and other substances have more time to diffuse into pores and adsorb onto sorption sites. text: This study investigated the sorption of per- and polyfluorinated-alkyl substances (PFAS) onto granular activated carbon (GAC). The study was performed at environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations and a realistic water-to-GAC ratio, providing a realism often overlooked in existing studies. Three different forms of GAC were evaluated, differing in micropore and mesopore structures. Tap water spiked with 5 ng/L of each of 31 PFAS was used in the sorption experiments, i.e. perfluorocarboxylic acids (C 4 – C 12 ), perfluorosulfonic acids (PFSA, C 5 – C 10 ) including linear and branched isomers, and three groups of PFAS precursors (per-/polyfluoroalkyl ether acids, sulfonamides, and sulfonamide acetic acids). The three studied GAC did not exhibit distinct differences in PFAS sorption. The removal of PFAS was below 50 % for most studied PFAS, except for the short-chain PFAS precursors. Sorption was affected by both the carbon chain length and functional groups for PFAS, while this was not observed for PFAS precursors. The presence of ether linkages and sulfonamide groups notably enhanced sorption. Linear and branched PFSA demonstrated similar sorption behavior, whereas branched isomers of the sulfonamide acetic acid precursors exhibited significantly higher sorp - tion. This indicates that sorption was determined by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions.

Dynamic adsorption pr oc esses Dynamic adsorption systems, including fixed-bed and fluidised- bed reactors, have been optimised for continuous flow applications, allowing for high-throughput treatment of PFAS- contaminated water. Fixed-bed columns packed with GAC, ion- exchange resins or functionalised biochar are widely employed in municipal and industrial settings (Khan et al. 2022). These systems enable prolonged contact between PFAS molecules and adsorbent surfaces, promoting effective removal. Fluidised-bed reactors, which maintain the adsorbent particles in a suspended state, improve mass transfer rates and reduce channeling, making them advantageous for treating large volumes of water. Emerging configurations, such as moving-bed and rotating-packed bed reactors, are being explored to further enhance kinetic performance, reduce energy consumption and manage hydraulic load (Bhutia et al. 2025). While it is true that GAC and PAC exhibit higher PFAS removal ef - ficiencies due to their superior BET surface area and adsorption per - formance, CFA offers several advantages that could offset its lower adsorption capacity. One significant advantage of CFA is its low cost and widespread availability, as it is an industrial byproduct commonly produced in large quantities. This makes CFA a cost-effective and sus - tainable choice, especially for large-scale applications where high vol - umes of adsorbent are needed. Also, the manufacturing of activated carbon involves high energy and chemical consumption and high carbon emission. text: Findings from this study examined for the ﬁrst time the adsorption of 75 PFASs from an AFFF mixture to 14 adsorbents (13 resins and GAC) at environmentally relevant concentrations. Results from this work show that AERs with polystyrene backbones are more selective toward PFASs compared to GAC, especially for the short-chain PFAAs (e.g., PFBA). Furthermore, by comparing the selectivity coe ﬃ cients of each PFAS −AER combination, the physical characteristics of AERs (i.e., polymer matrix, functional group, and morphology) were found to strongly inﬂuence their a ﬃ nity and capacity toward the 75 PFASs. For example, while macroporous AERs were found to exhibit a much higher maximum PFOS capacity compared to gel-type AERs, AERs that contain more hydrophobic polymer matrices (e.g., polystyrene) and functional groups (e.g., quaternary ammonium with long alkyl branches) tend to display stronger selectivity toward PFASs compared to other AERs that lack these properties. These ﬁndings con ﬁrm that rather than electrostatic interactions alone driving the adsorption process, nonelectrostatic interactions (e.g., hydrophobic interaction) played an important role in controlling the extent to which individual PFASs adsorb to di ﬀerent resins. Such ﬁndings are valuable assets for developing more e ﬀective AERs to treat the wide range of PFASs detected in the environment.

In all methods, the cleanup of extract to eliminate interfering organic and inorganic compounds prior to LC-MS/MS analysis is critical to obtaining acceptable chromatogram quality and recoveries of PFAS from these complex matrices. While a variety of adsorbents have been employed in the cleanup step, we argue that a “one-size-fits- all” method may not exist. Specifically, in this study, we observed that none of the existing methods could prevent precipitate formation when methanolic extracts from the five studied biosolids were reconstituted with water. Centrifugation and filtration of the reconstituted extracts to remove precipitates did not sufficiently eliminate interferences to allow PFAS quantification. To overcome this issue, the use of blends of adsorbents (ENVI-Carb, PSA, C18) with different adsorptive properties that could remove a broader range of interfering substances was evaluated. A blend consisting of 1000 mg ENVI-Carb, 500 mg PSA and 500 mg C18 was used to successfully analyze PFAS in the six studied biosolids. While this adsorbent formulation shows considerable promise, the optimum formulation could be sample-specific, given that sludges and biosolids vary widely in characteristics.

text: Electrochemical oxidation is generally employed downstream of concentration technologies such as IXR or foam fractionation rather than being applied directly to PFAS- impacted groundwater. This treatment sequence reflects several key constraints at environmentally relevant concen- trations. First, PFAS levels in groundwater typically span the ng L −1 to μg L −1 range, where mass transfer limitations restrict removal efficiency at the electrode surface. Second, the direct application of electrochemical oxidation to groundwater would require prohibitively large electrode areas and high energy input given the large water volumes involved, whereas treatment of concentrated residual streams enables more efficient operation. Third, because PFAS degradation by electrochemical oxidation follows approximately first-order kinetics, higher influent concentrations (mg L −1 ) are associated with reduced specific energy demand compared to μg L −1 influent levels. Conclusions This study examines the potential of electrochemical removal of PFAS, specifically, and FOCs in general, from water. This study explores the physical chemistry of the process, presenting both chemical and physical mechanisms, while developing a laboratory- scale separation process that operates in both batch and continuous modes. As this study concentrates on a proof-of-concept for continuous process development, it is quite distinct from earlier research using electrochemistry to eliminate PFAS. Those studies typically focus on batch experiments with much higher concentrations, so that the final residues remain within toxic ranges. Different FOCs were used to establish the electrochemical method, and all were removed from the solutions with high efficiency ( > 95%, in most cases). text: Electrochemical per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) removal from tap water: Proof-of-concept and laboratory scale pilot Phillip Vershinin 1 , * , Omri Seemann , Ishai Dror 2 , Brian Berkowitz 3 Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Fluorinated organic compounds Electrochemical degradation Water Treatment Batch process Continuous process ABSTRACT The removal of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from water remains a major envi - ronmental challenge, particularly at low concentrations (~ µ g L � 1 ) and in mixtures containing both long- and short-chain variants. This study focuses on developing an effective PFAS removal process using electrochemistry. A proof-of-concept for the removal of fluorinated organic com - pounds and PFAS from a controlled, clean environment is first demonstrated, and the removal mechanisms are clarified. A laboratory-scale batch system for PFAS removal was then designed and tested. Under realistic conditions (PFAS concentrations ~ 10 µ g L � 1 in tap water), PFAS concentrations were reduced significantly ( < 0.06 µ g L � 1 ) within a relatively short time (t ½ < 15 min) . A continuous stirred-tank reactor system was also developed to examine a continuous process.

Characteristics of organic and inorganic matters. Both organic com- pounds and inorganic ions are highly heterogenous, containing species with diﬀerent characteristics and consequently distinctive impacts on PFAS treatment. The molecular weight, functional groups, and hy- drophobicity are such speciﬁcations of organic matters leading to dif- ferent eﬀects on the eﬃcacy of physical-separation and degradation processes. Such characteristics of organic matters may aﬀect the com- petition for adsorption sites or surface properties of membranes. Adsorption onto activated carbon (AC) has been iden- tiﬁed as an effective technique to remove PFAS. Adsorption isotherms and breakthrough curves, determined by rapid small-scale column tests (RSSCTs), were studied for eight PFAS and four granular ACs, characterized by dif- ferent origins, porosities and numbers of reactivation cycles. Both batch and RSSCT results highlighted the strong interaction of AC and PFAS characteristics in adsorption capacity. The most important factor affecting AC perfor- mance is the surface charge: a positively-charged AC showed higher adsorption capacities with greater Freundlich constants (K F) and later 50% breakthroughs compared to the AC with neutral surface. doc_id: 2025 - Pavithra - Adsorption of Perfluorooctanoic Acid from Aqueous Media Using an Engineered Sugarcane Bagasse Biochar-Chitosan Composite.pdf
text: A Sustainable T echnology for Water T reatment Developed economies can afford advance techniques for removal of PFAS from water. However in developing countries, given the challenges of open drains or direct discharges releasing such persistent micropollutants in the water bodies, there is a basic need of a filter- ing medium using a low-cost adsorbent [25]. Cost-effective engineered SBCT composite can provide a solution for eliminating PFOA from wastewater or contaminated water bodies. This lab-scale study includes adsorption experiments using aqueous solutions, whereas real wastewater systems are far more complex. The presence of competing ions, dissolved organic matter, fluctuating pH, and variable contaminant loads may hinder adsorption effi- ciency and affect reproducibility under field conditions. It is to be noted, that the variability in the source, composition, and quality of raw materials, especially biochar precursors and https://doi.org/10.3390/chemengineering10020030 ChemEngineering 2026, 10, 30 16 of 21 biopolymer content, may affect the physicochemical properties and adsorption efficacy of the composite at larger scales. Consequently, the standardization of raw material selection and synthesis parameters will be crucial for ensuring uniform performance. Pilot-scale studies and long-term field trials using real wastewater matrices are required to validate the robustness and reliability of SBCT under realistic operating environments.
citation: Pavithra, K.; Chakraborty, P.. Adsorption of Perfluorooctanoic Acid from Aqueous Media Using an Engineered Sugarcane Bagasse Biochar–Chitosan Composite. ChemEngineering 2026 10 30. DOI: 10.3390/chemengineering10020030.

Due to their widespread use, PFAS have been detected in drinking water sources and various consumer products, which has raised significant concern since exposure to these contaminants is associated with various adverse health effects [9–12] . Because of their environmental persistence and negative human/ecological impacts, finding efficient approaches to eliminating PFAS is timely and essential. Among the various PFAS remediation methods, photo - induced approaches have recently emerged as promising techniques for the degradation of these contaminants [13 – 17] . doc_id: 2025 - Capodaglio - Prospects of Novel Technologies for PFAS Destruction in Water and Wastewater.pdf
text: AORP methods (photocatalysis, EAOP , NTP , E- beam), pyrolysis, and SCWO have been proposed to achieve the final destruction of PFAS compounds. Ongoing research aims at reducing the cost of these technologies and improving their destruction efficiency; commercial PFAS destruction methods have been introduced recently, but their full-scale application is still unreported in the scientific literature. Concerns about the potential for some PFASs and precursors to break through current treatment methods, the partial degradation of targeted compounds to non-targeted ones, and potentially dangerous by-products have not been dismissed yet, due to the non- detectability of a large number of PFAS molecules beyond those targeted by regulations. Incomplete and uncertain degradation pathways following destructive treatment also raise issues about overall risk reduction. A major challenge for the assessment of an effective reduction in PFAS contamination is related to the standardization of their quantification methodologies and to the development of analytical advancements to allow for the identification of PFAS congeners following specific treatments and fine-tune both removal and destructive remediation technologies. Generally speaking, the most effective technologies for breaking down PFASs are those that can rapidly deliver high energy into a contaminated solution, in order to overcome the high C-F bond strength and avoid by-product accumulation during the destruction process.

text: In this study, we developed an enhanced stir bar sorptive extraction (SBSE) method coupled with thermal desorption–gas chromatography– mass spectrometry (TD-GC-MS) for the analysis of PFCAs in water. This method demonstrates linearity, with R2 values from 0.9892 to 0.9988, and low limits of detection (LOD) between 21.17 ng/L and 73.96 ng/L. Recovery rates varied from 47 to 97%, suggesting efficient extraction. Compared to traditional methods, the developed SBSE technique requires only a 1 mL sample volume and minimal amounts of solvents, enhancing eco-friendliness and reducing potential contamination and handling errors. This method also demonstrated good precision and robustness across various water matrices. Overall, the developed method offers a precise, eco-friendly, and reliable approach for analyzing PFCAs in diverse water samples. Similar to sensor research, the selectivity of sorbents is crucial but hard to compare as it is greatly impacted by the experimental conditions. Furthermore, few papers of PFAS sorbents demonstrated and discussed the selectivity by comparing the adsorption performance between PFAS and its interferents individually; instead, most of them examined the selectivity as the anti-interferent ability by showing an una ﬀected PFAS adsorption performance in the presence of interferents. This method is not unreasonable in terms of demonstrating the selectivity, but at the same time, one should pay attention to the dosage of sorbents, the species of selected interferents, and the concentrations of all analytes in sample solutions and make sure the una ﬀected performance is not caused by overloading of sorbents or using unrealistic sample solutions. Since the adsorption performance is largely related to the initial concentration of PFAS analyte, all sorbents should be tested under environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations (ng/L to μg/L). However, most existing research conducted adsorption experiments in batch mode under unrealistic initial concentrations (>mg/L), 36,115 which cannot truly re ﬂect the capability of those sorbents in real applications. Furthermore, the performance of more sorbents, especially emerging ones, needs to be tested in the column mode, which is a closer proxy to practical environments.

text: Effect of batch and column studies Adsorption can be studied through batch and column methods, with batch studies being closed systems and column studies involving continuous sorbate flow ( Naboulsi et al., 2024 ). Batch studies are crucial for lab-scale investigations, providing initial insights into adsorbent performance and adsorption modeling but have limited practical rele - vance. In contrast, column studies better represent field conditions, supporting continuous pollutant removal, flow dynamics, and regener - ation studies. However, equilibrium in column studies is achieved only after the breakthrough point due to shorter contact times ( Sazali et al., 2020 ). Numerous studies have utilized batch and column experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of various biochars in treating different pol - lutants, providing comprehensive insights into the versatility of biochar in treatment applications. Huang et al. (2022a) reported a maximum sorption density of 2200 mg/kg for Al-modified bamboo biochar in a batch study, where the removal of sulfonamides occurred through electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic effects, and π - π interactions. While in the fixed-column study, the highest removal efficiency was achieved with a 1000 mg dose at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. The break - through model revealed that the adsorption process was primarily controlled by solid surface mass transfer and diffusion mechanisms.

text: In this study, rapid small-scale column tests (RSSCTs) were used to investigate the effects of PFAS type and chain length on adsorption by GAC and IX resin for six groundwaters used as drink- ing water supplies. text: GAC and PAC, which typically have high porosity and a large specific surface area, perform better on a mass basis because they can hold a larger amount of PFAS per gram, despite possibly lower adsorption per unit surface area compared to CFA. Thus, while CFA may have favorable surface characteristics, the higher adsorption capacities of GAC and PAC by mass indicate that they are more effective adsorbents overall for PFAS in bulk applications. Finally, the lower mass-based capacity of CFA can be conquered by applying higher dose since its minimal cost and environmental impact. While it is true that GAC and PAC exhibit higher PFAS removal ef - ficiencies due to their superior BET surface area and adsorption per - formance, CFA offers several advantages that could offset its lower adsorption capacity. One significant advantage of CFA is its low cost and widespread availability, as it is an industrial byproduct commonly produced in large quantities. This makes CFA a cost-effective and sus - tainable choice, especially for large-scale applications where high vol - umes of adsorbent are needed. Also, the manufacturing of activated carbon involves high energy and chemical consumption and high carbon emission. Additionally, the regeneration of activated carbon, while possible, may lead to a decrease in its adsorption efficiency over time and could potentially introduce secondary pollution risks through the desorption of previously adsorbed contaminants.

text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. It explores major contamination sources and pathways, highlights their global distribution and examines the evolving regulatory landscape. The review focuses on adsorption-based removal technologies, in-depth evaluating mechanisms of PFAS interactions with adsorbents such as activated carbon, biochar, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and ion-exchange resins. text: Findings from this study examined for the ﬁrst time the adsorption of 75 PFASs from an AFFF mixture to 14 adsorbents (13 resins and GAC) at environmentally relevant concentrations. Results from this work show that AERs with polystyrene backbones are more selective toward PFASs compared to GAC, especially for the short-chain PFAAs (e.g., PFBA). Furthermore, by comparing the selectivity coe ﬃ cients of each PFAS −AER combination, the physical characteristics of AERs (i.e., polymer matrix, functional group, and morphology) were found to strongly inﬂuence their a ﬃ nity and capacity toward the 75 PFASs. For example, while macroporous AERs were found to exhibit a much higher maximum PFOS capacity compared to gel-type AERs, AERs that contain more hydrophobic polymer matrices (e.g., polystyrene) and functional groups (e.g., quaternary ammonium with long alkyl branches) tend to display stronger selectivity toward PFASs compared to other AERs that lack these properties. These ﬁndings con ﬁrm that rather than electrostatic interactions alone driving the adsorption process, nonelectrostatic interactions (e.g., hydrophobic interaction) played an important role in controlling the extent to which individual PFASs adsorb to di ﬀerent resins. Such ﬁndings are valuable assets for developing more e ﬀective AERs to treat the wide range of PFASs detected in the environment.

text: PFAS are used in laboratory research to produce artificially contaminated feed water for convenience of measurement. The most commonly used for PFAS are adsorption (including ion exchange), membrane filtration, and degra- dation (Table 1). Adsorption is the simplest of these methods and relatively inexpensive (Lei et al. 2023). However, the cost and treatment time for adsorption increases if a strict removal rate needs to be achieved. Membrane treatment ensures a good removal rate for the permeate (T. Lee et al. 2022) but the energy needed to generate filtration pressure makes membrane treatment more expensive than adsorp- tion. Both adsorption and filtration concentrate, but do not destroy, PFAS. Degradation could be used to destroy PFAS, but high energy is needed to rupture PFAS molecules. Therefore, degradation is also expensive. Filtration treatment costs could be reduced by developing a membrane with a high permeable flux that maintains the PFAS blocking rate. Many general reviews have recently been published on PFAS treatment. Most existing reviews (Saawarn et al. 2022; Wanninayake 2021; Yadav et al. 2022) summarize different PFAS treatment methods, among which only a few studies on membrane-based methods are included. Some studies are being con- ducted on membrane distillation, adsorption, and degra- dation. Membrane filtration offers the advantage of a high PFAS removal rate but is not as widely applied as adsorp- tion because of cost constraints. This limitation could be overcome by experimenting with using different membrane preparation methods to increase the specific flux while maintaining the PFAS removal rate. The use of membranes with high specific fluxes can reduce electrical consumption and thereby, operation costs. A NF membrane with a specific flux of ~ 50 L/(m 2 h bar) and a 99% PFAS removal rate is promising for treatment. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) such as electrochemical oxidation, ozonation, UV-based systems, and supercritical water oxidation aim to degrade PFAS rather than separate them 15,16. Membrane separation processes are widely applied in water/waste - water treatment and industries and it was found to be effective in rejecting short and long chain PFAS with efficiencies exceeding 90 % [ 24 , 25 ]. Generally, in membrane separation systems, feed water con - taining PFAS molecules is rejected by the membrane (semi-permeable selective barrier) while water molecules are passing to the permeation side of the system. The most famous, effective and largely investigated membrane systems for PFAS removal are pressure driven membrane systems, particularly nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) sys - tems. The defined removal mechanism are size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution diffusion for NF and RO, respectively. The effi - ciency of these membranes in rejecting PFASs from aqueous environ - ments were reported to approach 99 % [ 26 , 27 ]. Despite the maturity level of the NF and RO systems and simplicity in application, the major drawback experienced is treatment of rejected streams containing high PFAS concentration which requires further attention by coupling membrane separation with other processes such as adsorption or AOPs.

The recalcitrant behavior of PFAS to most traditional water treatment processes calls for development of novel or modified treatment approaches for effective PFAS elimination. Currently, high- pressure membrane systems, including nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) are among the most promising and readily applied technologies for PFAS removal. In this review, we summarized peer-reviewed scientific articles on the development and use of 20 different types of commercial and 6 synthesized/modified NF and RO membranes in terms of PFAS removal efficacy. Synthesizing of existing knowledge shows that under environmentally relevant pH and concentration, NF and RO can effectively remove PFAS from water. The impact of PFAS molecular weight (MW) and functionality, membrane characteristics, feed water constitution, natural organic matters and operational conditions were systematically reviewed and evaluated. Moving forward, we recommend additional research dedicated to understanding the behaviors of PFAS alternatives and other over - looked compounds (e.g., PFAS with chain length C 2 and C3) during NF and RO processes. Further, it is critical to develop or optimize existing membrane products with strong selectivity for specific PFAS species, while being resistant to fouling. Recent advances in material science, process engineering and systems integration are driv - ing the development of novel adsorption platforms that not only enhance PFAS removal efficiency but also prioritise sustainability, scalability and cost-effectiveness. This section highlights five key areas of technological advancement in PFAS adsorption. Membra ne-based adsorption s ys tems Membrane-based adsorption technologies represent a prom - ising convergence of separation and adsorption processes. These systems incorporate functional adsorbents such as AC, CNTs, MOFs and ion-exchange resins into porous mem - branes, enabling simultaneous filtration and contaminant capture (Davoodbeygi et al. 2023). Owing to their high surface area and customisable pore structures, adsorptive membranes can effectively target both long- and short-chain PFASs, which are often inadequately removed by traditional techniques. Advanced hybrid membranes, including those functiona - lised with zwitterionic polymers or thin-film composites, offer enhanced selectivity by leveraging electrostatic, hydro - phobic and hydrogen bonding interactions (Gu et al. 2024). Zwitterionic electrospun membranes, for example, have demonstrated strong PFAS adsorption capacity while resist - ing fouling in complex matrices.
