In these cases, the treatment meth- odology is multistep requiring additional expenditure of energy along with cost associated with complexity. Direct decomposition is desirable in that ideally it does not create an additional waste stream; rather, the compound is disassembled chemically to harm- less by-products. Key questions regarding PFAS treatment include what is the fate of the shorter chains produced, and is the advanced method also appropriate to treat these shorter chains? Such ques- tions have not been settled to date. 8 In this work, plasma treatment is applied to the treatment of PFAS-contaminated ground water. While plasma treatment is often thought of as an advanced oxidation method, it has been shown that oxidation is not effective in decomposing short chain PFAS compounds. 8 This is largely due the relative strength of the C –F bond and the high electronegativity of fluorine. The oxidation potential of fluorine is larger than that of OH, the chief radical in advanced oxidation. Reduction methods, on the other hand, have shown success at defluorinating and ultimately decomposing PFAS compounds. 9 These methods feature solvated electrons —a short lived, highly reactive complex that destabilizes PFAS compounds.

text: PFAS ’ hydrophobic and oleophobic characteristics, chemical and mechanical stability, and strong resistance to bio - logical, chemical, and thermal degradation make them difficult to remove from aquatic settings. PFAS removal from aquatic environments using membrane technologies is promising due to their superior rejection of various PFAS categories and maturity level. This review article discusses membrane technologies ’ present trajectory to remove PFAS in water and wastewater treatment. Current advances in reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, membrane distillation, and adsorptive nanofiber membranes are examined, including their pros and cons. Hybrid tech - nologies that combine membrane technologies with non-destructive or destructive methods are promising PFAS removal methods. Along with scientific discourse, this review critically discusses techno-economic elements of single and hybrid membrane processes to determine their practicality and cost-efficiency for implementation. This paper covers the newest membrane technologies for PFAS cleanup. Additionally, it sheds light on this essential domain ’ s research prospects. 1. This treatment method is based on utilizing the property of PFAS molecules having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic components that leads to the concentra- tion of PFAS on the water-air interface. In foam fractionation, PFAS are concentrated in the foam, which forms on the water surface due to provided aeration. The foam is collected by overflow or by suction. The process is most often performed in batch mode ( Lee and Venkatesan, 2024 , Wang et al., 2023 ), although a continuous process is also possible ( Smith et al., 2022 ). The removed collapsed foam (foamate) is further concentrated by subsequent foam fractionation steps ( Burns et al., 2022 ) or treated by electrochemical oxidation ( Smith et al., 2023b ). These membrane systems are particularly well-suited for point-of-use and point-of- entry applications due to their compact form, operational efficiency and adaptability. However, challenges such as membrane fouling, fabrication costs and limited regenera - tion strategies remain areas of ongoing research. Dynamic adsorption pr oc esses Dynamic adsorption systems, including fixed-bed and fluidised- bed reactors, have been optimised for continuous flow applications, allowing for high-throughput treatment of PFAS- contaminated water. Fixed-bed columns packed with GAC, ion- exchange resins or functionalised biochar are widely employed in municipal and industrial settings (Khan et al. 2022). These systems enable prolonged contact between PFAS molecules and adsorbent surfaces, promoting effective removal. Fluidised-bed reactors, which maintain the adsorbent particles in a suspended state, improve mass transfer rates and reduce channeling, making them advantageous for treating large volumes of water. Emerging configurations, such as moving-bed and rotating-packed bed reactors, are being explored to further enhance kinetic performance, reduce energy consumption and manage hydraulic load (Bhutia et al. 2025). Although these systems are promising, their design must care - fully balance pressure drops, retention times and susceptibility to fouling by co-contaminants or suspended solids.

Membrane separation processes are widely applied in water/waste - water treatment and industries and it was found to be effective in rejecting short and long chain PFAS with efficiencies exceeding 90 % [ 24 , 25 ]. Generally, in membrane separation systems, feed water con - taining PFAS molecules is rejected by the membrane (semi-permeable selective barrier) while water molecules are passing to the permeation side of the system. The most famous, effective and largely investigated membrane systems for PFAS removal are pressure driven membrane systems, particularly nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) sys - tems. The defined removal mechanism are size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution diffusion for NF and RO, respectively. The effi - ciency of these membranes in rejecting PFASs from aqueous environ - ments were reported to approach 99 % [ 26 , 27 ]. Subcritical water temperatures range from 100 /C176 C to 350 /C176 C and are maintained at a certain pressure to hold a liquid state. In comparison, supercritical water temperatures reach >350/C176 C and pressures >22.1 MPa ( Jessop and Leitner, 1999). At these temperatures and pres- sures, sub- and supercritical water has useful properties for degrading hazardous compounds, including high diffusivity and low viscosity. Plasma is formed by applying a su ﬃ ciently high electrical potential between the high voltage and grounded electrodes via an external plasma-generating network. Argon gas is pumped through submerged di ﬀusers to produce bubbles and form a layer of foam on the liquid surface. This foam concentrates surfactant-like contaminants (e.g., PFAS) and enhances the contact between the liquid and the plasma, exposing the contaminant at the gas −liquid interface to reactive oxidative and reductive species in the plasma. 21 Unlike other AOPs which are solely based on the production of OH radicals, plasma treatment involves generation of reductive species (hot and aqueous electrons, hydrogen radicals) and ions (e.g., argon ions) without requiring any chemical inputs. The recalcitrant behavior of PFAS to most traditional water treatment processes calls for development of novel or modified treatment approaches for effective PFAS elimination. Currently, high- pressure membrane systems, including nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) are among the most promising and readily applied technologies for PFAS removal. In this review, we summarized peer-reviewed scientific articles on the development and use of 20 different types of commercial and 6 synthesized/modified NF and RO membranes in terms of PFAS removal efficacy. Moving forward, we recommend additional research dedicated to understanding the behaviors of PFAS alternatives and other over - looked compounds (e.g., PFAS with chain length C 2 and C3) during NF and RO processes. ARTICLE INFO Editor: Jay Gan Keywords: PFAS Immobilization Adsorption;, soil remediation Water treatment ABSTRACT Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) present significant environmental and health hazards due to their inherent persistence, ubiquitous presence in the environment, and propensity for bioaccumulation. Conse- quently, the development of efficacious remediation strategies for soil and water contaminated with PFAS is imperative. Biochar, with its unique properties, has emerged as a cost-effective adsorbent for PFAS. Despite this, a comprehensive review of the factors influencing PFAS adsorption and immobilization by biochar is lacking. This narrative review examines recent findings indicating that the application of biochar can effectively immobilize PFAS, thereby mitigating their environmental transport and subsequent ecological impact. In addi- tion, this paper reviewed the sorption mechanisms of biochar and the factors affecting its sorption efficiency. The high effectiveness of biochars in PFAS remediation has been attributed to their high porosity in the right pore size range ( > 1.5 nm) that can accommodate the relatively large PFAS molecules ( > 1.02 – 2.20 nm), leading to physical entrapment. Effective sorption requires attraction or bonding to the biochar framework. ABSTRACT: Currently, there is an increasing interest in developing efficient and cost-effective treatment technologies to remediate per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in water. Biochars (pristine and modified/engineered) can be a good candidate among porous pyrogenic carbonaceous materials for the sorptive removal of PFAS from water/wastewater. Regeneration of spent adsorbent after PFAS adsorption Managing spent adsorbents presents environmental and economic challenges, primarily due to the risk of rein- troducing PFAS into the environment during disposal or regeneration. Advanced regeneration techniques, such as microwave, chemical, thermal, and hydrothermal treatments, have shown promising potential, achieving up to w99 % regeneration efﬁciency for PFAS-laden carbon-based composites [ 50]. Chemical regeneration is particularly effective for multicomponent regenerates and has demonstrated durability over ﬁve consecutive adsorptionedesorption cycles. However, combining chemical regeneration with advanced degradation sys- tems, while effective, often reduces PFAS adsorption capacity by 5 e10 % due to irreversible adsorption and pore blocking. Thermal regeneration, performed at high temperatures (/C21700e800 /C14C), has proven effective but is unsuitable for certain adsorbents, such as ion- exchange resins, due to structural degradation under extreme conditions. These limitations highlight the need for innovative, cost-effective regeneration strate- gies tailored to the speciﬁc properties of adsorbents and the type of PFAS contamination being addressed. text: In this study, we demonstrate a simple way to activate and reactivate biochar to effectively remove PFAS from water. At low pH, MER generated stable foam, with PFAS–organic complexes adsorbing at the air–water interface, reducing surface tension and preventing foam collapse. text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. The removal of PFAS by GAC can be explained by several mecha - nisms, including hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic attraction, and PFAS aggregation ( Du et al., 2014 ). PFAS compounds vary significantly in hydrophobicity: carbon chain length is proportional to hydropho - bicity, and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) demonstrate increased hydrophobicity as compared to perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) with the same perfluorinated carbon chain length ( Park et al., 2020 ). As such, GAC treatment has been found to be more effective for removing longer-chain PFAS than shorter-chain ones, and more effective for removing PFSA than PFCA ( McCleaf et al., 2017; Westreich et al., 2018 ). Traditional full-scale GAC treatment facility design is typically based on empty bed contact time (EBCT) and media service-life, often described by the number of bed volumes (BVs) the system can treat until solute breakthrough ( Crittenden et al., 1987 ). Environmental implication The urgent global issue of PFAS contamination necessitates effective remediation strategies. Current methods primarily rely on carbon-based adsorbents such as granular activated carbon, which, while effective, impose significant environmental and energy burdens during manufacturing. Simultaneously, coal fly ash, a byproduct of the coal power industry, presents its own environmental challenges. This study stands as one of the pioneering efforts to utilize coal fly ash as an adsorbent for the removal of PFAS from landfill leachate. Introduction Water above 374°C and 22.1 MPa becomes supercritical, a special phase of water with both liquid-like and gas-like properties. Above the critical point of water, most organic compounds are soluble, oxygen is fully miscible, and salts are insoluble ( Hodes et al. 2004 ; V oisin et al. 2017). In the presence of an oxidizing agent, such as oxygen, supercritical water ’s unique properties accelerate the oxidation of a broad range of organic pollutants. Since the 1980s, supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) has been used successfully to treat a variety of hazardous wastes, such as chemical warfare agents and halogenated compounds ( Abeln et al. 2001 ; Cohen et al. 1998 ; Kim et al. 2010 ). Higher temperatures are needed to achieve higher destruction efficiencies, which translates to longer heat-up times, and increased energy inputs. From a thermodynamic standpoint, the energetic requirements for SCWO are comparable to incineration of wet wastes. Under atmospheric conditions ~2600 kJ/kg of energy input is required to heat and evap - orate water from 20 ◦ C to 100 ◦ C, while heating and pressurizing water from 20 ◦ C to the supercritical phase at 25 MPa and 500 ◦ C requires ~3060 kJ/kg ( Lemmon et al., 2018 ). Under oxidizing conditions, both SCWO and incineration valorize the energetic content of the feedstock to reduce overall energy demand. SCWO does not produce particulate matter (PM), NO x or SO 2 as reaction products due to the lower operating temperatures, which eliminates the emission treatment requirements on industrial incinerators. In light of these findings, continuous SCWO processing seems more promising than batch SCWO processing as an end-of-life disposal process for PFAS-rich wastes. Continuous SCWO processing requires the PFAS to be contained in a liquid matrix with low salt content to avoid issues with scaling and corrosion.

This residual loading can cause pre- mature breakthrough in service, risking exceedances of the PFAS limits unless regeneration cycles are more effective or more frequent. Thermal destruction, while capable of >95% Water 2025, 17, 2813 18 of 28 PFAS mineralisation under controlled laboratory conditions, raises concerns regarding the scalability and completeness of destruction under real-world conditions, particularly with respect to HF and other fluorinated by-products that require advanced flue gas cleaning to meet POPs Regulation requirements [23,52,78,133,134]. EU environmental policy implicitly demands that PFAS releases are prevented not only during water treatment but also during all handling, regeneration, and end-of-life management steps. text: This review presents a comprehensive summary of several categories of treatme nt approaches: (1) sorption using activated carbon, ion exchange, or other sorbents, (2) advanced oxidation processes, including electrochemical oxidation, photolysis, and photocatalysis, (3) advanced reduction processes using a queous iodide or dithionite and sulﬁte, (4) thermal and nonthermal destruction, including incineration, sonochemical degradation, sub- or supercritical treatment, microwave- hydrothermal treatment, and high-voltage electric discharge, (5) microbial treatment, and (6) other treatment processes, including ozonation under alkaline conditions, permanganate oxidation, vitamin-B 12 and Ti(III) citrate reductive deﬂuorination, and ball milling. Discussion of each treatment technology, including background, mechanisms, ad- vances, and effectiveness, will informthe development of cost-effective PFAS remediation strategies based on envi- ronmental parameters and applicable methodologies. Further optimization of current technologies to analyze and remove or destroy PFASs below regulatory guidelines is needed. Due to the stability of PFASs, a combination of multiple treatment technologies will likely be required to effectively address real-world complexities of PFAS mixtures and cocontaminants present in environmental matrices. Supercritical water treatment Above its critical point (T c = 374 ◦ C, P c = 22.1 MPa), water becomes a non-polar solvent, which can efficiently dissolve organic substances and gases [36] . The ion product constant of supercritical water (SCW) is over five orders of magnitude lower than that of water at ambient conditions, facilitating free radical reaction pathways [37] which have been utilized in gasification [38 – 40] , partial oxidation [41] , and SCWO [42 – 44] processes. SCWO process benefits from the high free radical environment to convert organic compounds via oxidative reaction mechanisms into CO 2 and H 2 O, with the hydroxyl radical (OH*) being the primary oxidizing species [45 – 49] . Heteroatoms are converted to corresponding inorganic acids or salts, such as HCl, HF, sulfates, phosphates, etc. High-density homogeneous SCWO environment facilitates fast and more complete oxidative reactions. Water as the reaction medium allows for simulta - neous oxidation and hydrolysis mechanisms [50] , enabling the more complete destruction of some recalcitrant wastes.

By containing a fluorinated carbon tail and a hy- drophilic head (-COOH, -SO3H), PFASs act as surfactants that are attracted to bubble–water interfaces. Foam fractionation is the process of facilitating PFAS–air bubble interactions for the purpose of removing contaminants from tainted water. In this paper, we report on the use of foam fractionation and electrochemical oxidation (EO) under stirred batch conditions (200 mL) to remediate PFAS-contaminated water.

text: Microbial biodegradation Microbial biodegradation of PFAS primarily involves bacteria, which have shown varying capacities to transform and degrade these com - pounds under different environmental conditions. High concentrations of PFAS do not exhibit toxicity to microbial activity during biodegra - dation, often using activated sludge from wastewater treatment plants as a test medium [ 180 ]. The biological removal mechanism of PFAS relies on the initial biotransformation of vulnerable functional groups and reductive defluorination, processes carried out by specific bacteria. Microorganisms such as Acidimicrobium sp. A6, Pseudomonas and Rho - dococcus use metabolic pathways to attack the weak points of PFAS molecules, transforming them into less fluorinated intermediate prod - ucts, such as perfluoroalkyl acids (PFCAs) and shorter sulfonates. Under anaerobic conditions, certain bacteria can break carbon‑fluorine (C – F) bonds by reductive defluorination, releasing fluorine ions (F - ). These reactions are catalyzed by specialized enzymes, such as oxidoreductases and desulfonases. The processes are slow and incomplete, generating intermediate products that can still be persistent in the environment ( Fig. 4 A) [ 176 ]. Sorn et al. text: Simulation details In this study, a reactive molecular dynamics approach was employed alongside the ReaxFF reactive force field to simulate the decomposition behavior of PFNA under pyrolysis and supercritical water oxidation conditions. The simulation system was configured with a three- dimensional periodic boundary condition (PBC) to ensure adequate representation of the system and accuracy in kinetic behavior. The reactive force field used was based on the ReaxFF force field developed by Wood et al. [57] , applicable to elements such as C, H, O, S, F, Cl, and N. Key parameters were reparameterized within the JAX-ReaxFF framework, and the quantum chemical benchmark data necessary for parameter training were obtained through density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The B3LYP functional and 6 – 311 + + g(d,p) basis set were employed to validate the rationality of the reaction pathways and energy barriers [58,59] . Fig. 1 shows the supercell model constructed for pyrolysis and the supercritical water environment, along with the geometrically optimized structure of the PFNA molecule. text: This confirmed that PFASs were vapourised from biosolids at pyrolysis temperature leading to the production of nearly PFAS free biochar. Similar findings were published by Bioforcetech. 63,64 The extremely low concentrations of PFAS species in both biochar and scrubber water suggest that several PFAS species might have been partially or completely destroyed in the integrated pyrolysis –combustion environment maintained in the pyrolysis reactor and its adjacent annular space. Temperature, gas residence time, oxygen, water vapour and the gas phase chemistry of alkali and alkaline earth minerals ( i.e. K, Na, Ca, and Mg) might have played critical roles in PFAS destruction followed by mineralisation. The roles of temperature and residence time are well-known as higher temperature and residence times can improve the destruction kinetics. 65 The literature has demonstrated that oxygen and water vapour can play critical roles in the destruction of fluorinated hydrocarbons. 66,67 In a similar way, oxygen and water vapour (generated from combustion of pyrolysis gas vapours) can play important roles in PFAS destruction. The release of alkali and alkaline earth minerals into the vapour phase and their gas phase chemistry with PFASs and destructed fluorine can also enhance PFAS destruction and mineralisation efficiency. 66,68 There is also a possibility that PFASs might have converted into some unknown organofluorine compounds which might not be in the analytical range.

text: * Correspondence: e.hassan@msstate.edu; Tel.: +1-(662)325-8344 Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are a broad group of synthetic chemicals characterized by strong carbon–fluorine bonds, making them highly persistent and widely distributed in the environment. Their chain length and functional head groups, such as sulfonate and carboxylate groups, determine key molecular properties like hydrophobicity, acidity, and sorption behavior. These properties significantly impact the effectiveness of PFAS removal from water systems. This review provides a structural classification of PFASs and explores removal strategies, with a particular emphasis on adsorption. It examines sustainable adsorbents, including both natural materials (e.g., cellulose, chitosan, lignin, and cyclodextrins) and engineered synthetic materials (e.g., covalent organic frameworks, metal–organic frameworks, and molecularly imprinted polymers). The discussion highlights important parameters such as chain length and functional chemistry, as these can greatly influence removal efficiency. Furthermore, the discussion addresses the adsorption mechanisms-such as electrostatic attraction, hydrophobic interaction, and fluorophilic interactions-to show how they contribute in different systems. By combining structural insights with adsorption performance data, this review aims to help design and select sustainable, high-performance adsorbents for efficiently reducing PFASs in contaminated water.

Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. This review centers on current and emerging PFAS remediation strategies, which are mainly divided into destructive and non-destructive methods. Particular focus is placed on adsorption-based removal technologies, especially those using sustainable and synthetic polymeric adsorbents. We carefully evaluate the design, functionalization, and performance of these polymers in capturing PFASs from contaminated environments. Key factors affecting PFAS adsorption, such as chain length, head group chemistry, and the interaction between these molecular features and the adsorption mechanisms, are thoroughly discussed. We explain how the combination of chain length and head group polarity influences the affinity of PFAS molecules for different adsorbent surfaces, ulti- mately impacting removal efficiency. There are three reasons to focus on adsorption: First, it is a non-destructive method that does not produce secondary pollutants. Second, adsorption is simple in both the syn- thesis of adsorbents and their use. By contrast, nano-engineered adsorbents and hybrid materials, due to their high surface-to-volume ratios and reactive interfaces, tend to exhibit rapid uptake, often reaching equilibrium within min - utes (Birch et al. 2022). Rapid adsorption kinetics are essential for developing efficient point-of-use treatment technologies and scaling up continuous treatment systems. NOM may introduce steric hindrance, reduce porosity through fouling or shift surface charges, thereby diminishing PFAS removal efficiency (Qi et al. 2022). The removal of PFAS by GAC can be explained by several mecha - nisms, including hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic attraction, and PFAS aggregation ( Du et al., 2014 ). PFAS compounds vary significantly in hydrophobicity: carbon chain length is proportional to hydropho - bicity, and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA) demonstrate increased hydrophobicity as compared to perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) with the same perfluorinated carbon chain length ( Park et al., 2020 ). While GAC is a low-cost media, its performance is limited by rapid bed exhaustion, a large requisite contact time, and significant inhibition by groundwater co-constituents like natural organic matter (NOM) ( Du et al., 2014 ; Kothawala et al., 2017 ). This leads to high media usage rates, necessitating frequent replacement and off-site disposal or regeneration of large quantities of sorbent media ( Rahman et al., 2014 ). An alternative to GAC, anion exchange resins (AERs) are receiving increased attention for PFAS treatment. Conventional AERs used in water treatment (e.g., for nitrate) are often regenerable using a concentrated salt brine (e.g., 5-10% NaCl) to reverse the equilibrium and recover the resin ’ s adsorption capacity. However, strong affinity be - tween PFASs and AERs necessitates the addition of organic cosolvent to salt brines (e.g., 70% methanol in NaCl brine) to regenerate resins ( Boyer et al., 2021 ). Recently, resin manufacturers have introduced AERs with very high affinities for PFASs that are operated as single-use products designed to be disposed or incinerated upon exhaustion ( Boodoo et al., 2019 ).

Contact time is considered an important design parameter for sorption because it is crucial that the contact time is long enough to fully sorb the target contaminants ( Murray et al., 2021 , Pannu et al., 2024 ). Failure to optimize contact time can result in either inefficient removal of target contaminants or unnecessary cost of oper - ation. Therefore, selection of the appropriate contact time is essential for testing and scale-up of novel sorbents ( Murphy et al., 2023 ). The rec - ommended full-scale contact time for removing PFAS by conventional adsorbents is well studied, with a recommended contact time of 2 – 5 min for IX resins and 10 – 30 min for GAC ( Pannu et al., 2024 ). However, the optimal contact time is unknown for novel adsorbents. Therefore, this study focuses on understanding how contact time impacts breakthrough of contaminant mixtures in packed beds of StyDex in wastewater, and the implications for scaling-up to pilot and full-scale operations. Contact time and adsorption kinetics Adsorption kinetics influence the practicality of PFAS removal, especially in flow-through systems. Traditional adsorbents such as PAC often require extended contact times (up to several hours) to reach equilibrium (Son and An 2022). By contrast, nano-engineered adsorbents and hybrid materials, due to their high surface-to-volume ratios and reactive interfaces, tend to exhibit rapid uptake, often reaching equilibrium within min - utes (Birch et al. 2022). Rapid adsorption kinetics are essential for developing efficient point-of-use treatment technologies and scaling up continuous treatment systems. Pr esenc e of na tur al or ganic ma t ter (NOM) NOM, including humic and fulvic acids, can adversely affect PFAS adsorption by competing for active sites or altering adsorbent surface properties. NOM may introduce steric hindrance, reduce porosity through fouling or shift surface charges, thereby diminishing PFAS removal efficiency (Qi et al. 2022). Strategies such as pre-filtration, adsorbent surface modification or the development of anti-fouling materials can help mitigate these effects and improve per - formance in natural water matrices. text: This study investigated the sorption of per- and polyfluorinated-alkyl substances (PFAS) onto granular activated carbon (GAC). The study was performed at environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations and a realistic water-to-GAC ratio, providing a realism often overlooked in existing studies. Three different forms of GAC were evaluated, differing in micropore and mesopore structures. Tap water spiked with 5 ng/L of each of 31 PFAS was used in the sorption experiments, i.e. perfluorocarboxylic acids (C 4 – C 12 ), perfluorosulfonic acids (PFSA, C 5 – C 10 ) including linear and branched isomers, and three groups of PFAS precursors (per-/polyfluoroalkyl ether acids, sulfonamides, and sulfonamide acetic acids). The three studied GAC did not exhibit distinct differences in PFAS sorption. The removal of PFAS was below 50 % for most studied PFAS, except for the short-chain PFAS precursors. Sorption was affected by both the carbon chain length and functional groups for PFAS, while this was not observed for PFAS precursors. The presence of ether linkages and sulfonamide groups notably enhanced sorption. Linear and branched PFSA demonstrated similar sorption behavior, whereas branched isomers of the sulfonamide acetic acid precursors exhibited significantly higher sorp - tion. This indicates that sorption was determined by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions.

These membrane systems are particularly well-suited for point-of-use and point-of- entry applications due to their compact form, operational efficiency and adaptability. However, challenges such as membrane fouling, fabrication costs and limited regenera - tion strategies remain areas of ongoing research. Dynamic adsorption pr oc esses Dynamic adsorption systems, including fixed-bed and fluidised- bed reactors, have been optimised for continuous flow applications, allowing for high-throughput treatment of PFAS- contaminated water. Fixed-bed columns packed with GAC, ion- exchange resins or functionalised biochar are widely employed in municipal and industrial settings (Khan et al. 2022). These systems enable prolonged contact between PFAS molecules and adsorbent surfaces, promoting effective removal. Fluidised-bed reactors, which maintain the adsorbent particles in a suspended state, improve mass transfer rates and reduce channeling, making them advantageous for treating large volumes of water. Emerging configurations, such as moving-bed and rotating-packed bed reactors, are being explored to further enhance kinetic performance, reduce energy consumption and manage hydraulic load (Bhutia et al. 2025). Although these systems are promising, their design must care - fully balance pressure drops, retention times and susceptibility to fouling by co-contaminants or suspended solids.

text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. text: Findings from this study examined for the ﬁrst time the adsorption of 75 PFASs from an AFFF mixture to 14 adsorbents (13 resins and GAC) at environmentally relevant concentrations. Results from this work show that AERs with polystyrene backbones are more selective toward PFASs compared to GAC, especially for the short-chain PFAAs (e.g., PFBA). Furthermore, by comparing the selectivity coe ﬃ cients of each PFAS −AER combination, the physical characteristics of AERs (i.e., polymer matrix, functional group, and morphology) were found to strongly inﬂuence their a ﬃ nity and capacity toward the 75 PFASs. For example, while macroporous AERs were found to exhibit a much higher maximum PFOS capacity compared to gel-type AERs, AERs that contain more hydrophobic polymer matrices (e.g., polystyrene) and functional groups (e.g., quaternary ammonium with long alkyl branches) tend to display stronger selectivity toward PFASs compared to other AERs that lack these properties. These ﬁndings con ﬁrm that rather than electrostatic interactions alone driving the adsorption process, nonelectrostatic interactions (e.g., hydrophobic interaction) played an important role in controlling the extent to which individual PFASs adsorb to di ﬀerent resins. Such ﬁndings are valuable assets for developing more e ﬀective AERs to treat the wide range of PFASs detected in the environment.
